The SHM1 airfoil is integral to the design of the Honda business jet.
Natural laminar flow airfoils can offer a potential tenfold reduction in friction drag compared to turbulent boundary layers.
The numerical simulations solve the two-dimensional compressible Navier-Stokes equations using dispersion relation-preserving compact schemes.
The computational domain employs an O-grid topology with 1251 points in the azimuthal direction and 401 points in the wall-normal direction.
The free-stream Mach numbers (M_s) investigated range from 0.134 to 0.78, covering low speed, climb, cruise, and off-design transonic conditions.
The free-stream Reynolds number (Re_∞) ranges from 4.8 × 10^6 to 16.2 × 10^6.
The numerical results are validated against experimental flight test data from Fujino et al. for the SHM1 airfoil.
At the cruise condition (M_s = 0.62), the pressure distribution on the SHM1 airfoil shows a flat plateau on the suction surface, characteristic of natural laminar airfoils.
For the off-design transonic conditions, a pressure spike is observed at the shock location, with the steepest spike occurring for the shock-induced separation case at M_s = 0.78.
The vorticity spectrum becomes more chaotic and multi-periodic as the Mach number is increased, due to the nonlinear interactions between Kutta waves and the boundary layer.

The design conditions maintain a favorable pressure gradient and avoid flow separation, leading to lower drag, while the off-design transonic conditions experience strong shock waves and shock-induced separation, resulting in higher drag and unsteady aerodynamic loads.

The numerical approach used in this study implements an error-free non-overlapping parallelization strategy, which maintains the same level of accuracy as sequential computing through global spectral analysis.

The key objectives of this study are to provide a comprehensive assessment of the aerodynamic performance of the SHM1 airfoil under both design and off-design conditions, which can serve as a benchmark for future validation efforts.
The study aims to establish a foundation for strategies aimed at controlling flow separation and shocks to minimize friction drag on the SHM1 airfoil.
The natural laminar flow technology integrated with the SHM1 airfoil has gained relevance in modern commercial aircraft, business jets, and unmanned aerial vehicles.
